Adaptive long/short-term fusion is established prior art. [SLi-Rec (IJCAI 2019)](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2019/585) combines long-term preferences with a time/content-aware recurrent short-term representation through context-dependent attention. [CLSR (WWW 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13090) disentangles the two interests using contrastive supervision, then adaptively aggregates them. These precedents weaken novelty claims based solely on a learned fusion gate; a shared NextItNet encoder with different context windows would need a more specific contribution. Searches did not identify a clearly matching recommendation paper titled “Competing Interests Networks.”

[TLSRec (CIKM 2022)](https://yneversky.github.io/Papers/cikm22.pdf) supplies a directly relevant control: replace its neural time gate with equal averaging of long/short embeddings; it also compares single-head and multi-head attention fusion. The reported full model outperforms those replacements. This supports testing adaptive fusion against fixed averaging, but does not establish that gains in a different backbone come from context selection rather than normalization or capacity.

Recommended controls for the proposed single-network NextItNet extension: full-history-only and short-context-only models; fixed interpolation with its coefficient selected on validation; a learned global scalar versus an input-dependent gate; identical branch/output normalization across variants; and a parameter-matched full-history baseline. Keep shared encoder weights, embedding dimensions, scoring, training budget and validation candidates consistent. Treat these as proposed experimental controls, not ablations verified in the cited papers. Evidence for adaptive context selection requires gains over both tuned fixed interpolation and normalization/capacity-matched controls.
